1️⃣ Give the round one objective.

Choose balance, distance, defense, or a specific setup.

2️⃣ Repeat a simple combination.

Get familiar enough with it to notice the details.

3️⃣ Pick an actual target.

4️⃣ Manage your distance.

6️⃣ Build in a defensive response.

7️⃣ Film one round. Review one thing.

Here's the real secrets... 👇

1. Stop hitting every strike at 100%.

When everything is hard, everything becomes tense, slow, and predictable. Stay relaxed and choose when to add power.

2. Throw fewer strikes—but make them clean.
A sloppy eight-strike combination isn’t automatically better than a sharp three-strike combination.

3. Pause long enough to reset your stance.
If you finish every combination off-balance, you’re practicing a bad habit. Reset before attacking again.

4. Let the bag swing.
Don’t chase it around mindlessly. Use its movement to practice controlling range, cutting angles, and choosing when to engage.

5. Add defense after every combination.
Block, check, slip, frame, pivot, or move your feet. Your exchange isn’t finished just because you stopped striking.

6. Repeat one skill until it feels automatic.
You don’t need 50 combinations. Pick one weakness and give the round a specific purpose.

7. Stop before fatigue destroys your technique.
Getting tired can be part of the workout—but exhaustion isn’t proof that you improved.

Smart bag work can look slower and less dramatic.
But the goal isn’t to win a fight against the bag.
It’s to build habits that still work when someone hits back.

This is what I wish I knew when I first started… 👇

Most guys over 35 who want to start Muay Thai never actually walk into a gym.

They think about it for months. Sometimes years.

They watch reels. They Google gyms in their area. They buy a pair of wraps and let them sit in a drawer.

And every year that passes, the same voice gets louder.

Am I too old for this?

Here’s what nobody tells you.

Starting Muay Thai at 35+ isn’t the disadvantage everyone thinks it is. But there are 3 things you have to get right or you’ll quit within 6 months like most guys do.

1️⃣ Stop trying to train like a 22 year old.

You have a job, kids, and a body that doesn’t recover in 4 hours anymore. Three focused sessions a week beats six sloppy ones. Every time.

2️⃣ Get on a program before you get on the mat.

Walking into a gym cold is fine. Walking in with a base level of conditioning and some basic mechanics is better. You’ll be less sore, less embarrassed, and less likely to quit after your first tough class.

3️⃣ Protect your body like it’s a job.

Warm ups aren’t optional after 35. Neither is sleep, mobility, or knowing when to sit a hard sparring round out. The guys still training at 50 figured this out early.

Do those three things and here’s what happens.

Six months in, you’ll throw a kick that actually feels right for the first time.

A year in, you’ll be in the best shape you’ve been in since your 20s.

Two years in, you’ll be sparring guys 15 years younger and holding your own.

And five years in, you won’t recognize the version of yourself that spent months thinking about starting.

The clock’s going to keep moving either way.

You’ll be 40. You’ll be 45.

The only question is whether you’ll be a 45 year old who trains or a 45 year old who wishes he did.

Honestly, how many of these do you do 👇

1️⃣ They lift heavy 2 days a week, then fully rest. Not because they’re lazy. Because strength built with real recovery is what shows up in the late rounds.

2️⃣ They foam roll their hips before bed. Not because they’re sore. Because tight hips cap your kicks and your shots, and nobody talks about it.

3️⃣ They do 10 minutes of mobility every single day. Not because it’s fun. Because the fighter who’s still moving well in week 12 beats the one who’s nursing something.

4️⃣ They lay legs up the wall for 10 minutes after training. Not because it feels good. Because pooled blood in your legs kills tomorrow’s session before it starts.

5️⃣ They train explosiveness, not just endurance. Not because it looks cool. Because power off the ground is what separates a hard shot from a fight-ending one.

6️⃣ They rewatch their own rounds on film. Not because they’re vain. Because you can’t fix what you can’t see.

7️⃣ They drink water before coffee every morning. Not because they read it somewhere. Because dehydrated muscles fire slower. It’s that simple.

8️⃣ They breathe through their nose during warm-ups. Not because it’s easy. Because it trains your nervous system to stay calm when the pressure’s on.

9️⃣ They add 15 minutes to every warm-up nobody sees. Not because they’re early. Because that’s where the athleticism actually lives.

🔟 They program their strength in phases. 
Not because it’s complicated. Because building strength, then power, then explosiveness in order is what makes you peak instead of plateau.

The habits that look like nothing are doing everything.

Here’s the secret training plan... 👇

Actually, sorry. There is no “secret” or magic involved. Just structure and actually following it.

1️⃣ Muay Thai: 4x a week. Technique early when you’re fresh, hard sparring and pads later. Skill on fresh legs, conditioning when you’re tired.

2️⃣ Strength: 3x a week, in 30-day phases. First 30 days strength (heavy compounds). Days 30 to 60 power (move it with speed). Days 60 to 90 explosiveness (jumps, throws, fight-ready). It builds on itself.

3️⃣ Cardio: 2x a week. One long and easy to build the engine. One short and brutal for the gas tank. Most people skip the easy one and fade in round 3.

4️⃣ Mobility: 10 min daily. Hips, ankles, shoulders. Boring, and the reason you’re still training in week 12.

5️⃣ Nutrition: Protein every meal, real food, water dialed. You can’t out-train a bad diet or recover from one.

None of these are special on their own. The result comes from doing all five, in order, for 90 straight days.

The plan beats the effort every time. Structure is the whole game.

Try these “secrets” 👇

1️⃣ Keeping your hands a little low. Looks arrogant, like you’re asking to get hit. Actually it’s how you bait openings, stay relaxed, and react faster. Done with intention, not laziness.

2️⃣ Walking your opponent down slowly. Looks like showboating. Actually you’re controlling the pace, reading their rhythm, and making them fight your fight.

3️⃣ Throwing a teep like you’re bored. Looks dismissive. Actually one of the smartest range-control tools in the sport, and the calmer it looks, the better it’s working.

4️⃣ Standing tall and loose in the pocket. Looks cocky. Actually relaxed shoulders mean faster hands and more endurance deep into the rounds.

5️⃣ Taking the smile-and-nod after eating a shot. Looks like ego. Actually it resets your mind, hides the damage, and keeps you from fighting emotional.

6️⃣ Switching stance mid-exchange. Looks flashy. Actually it scrambles their reads and opens angles they didn’t see coming.

7️⃣ Pawing with the lead hand instead of throwing hard. Looks lazy and cocky. Actually you’re measuring distance and setting traps before the real shot.

8️⃣ Standing tall and loose in the pocket... wait, that’s taken. That little shoulder roll or shimmy. Looks like you’re playing. Actually it disguises your intentions and keeps you loose instead of stiff.

9️⃣ Going light when your partner’s going hard. Looks like you’re above it. Actually you’re building timing and technique that hold up when you’re exhausted.

🔟 Clinching and just... resting there. Looks like stalling. Actually you’re controlling posture, draining their energy, and dictating where the fight goes.

The guys who look like they’re trying the hardest are often improving the slowest. The ones who look calm and a little cocky? They’re getting dangerous quietly.

Muay Thai builds your skills and your engine. It does not build your body. If you want to actually look like you train, that comes from structured strength and conditioning, not more rounds.

Every fight camp I ran followed the same 12-week structure:

Weeks 1-4: Foundation. Build the base, clean up movement and mobility, lay the conditioning groundwork.

Weeks 5-8: Strength and power. Intensity climbs, and this is where the body actually starts to change.

Weeks 9-12: Peak. Lean, conditioned, and looking like a fighter, not just training like one.

30 to 40 minutes, 2-3 times a week, on top of your regular Muay Thai. That’s it. That’s the whole difference between looking like you train and looking like a fighter.

Let me explain... 👇

For years I thought more was the answer. More sessions, more rounds, more sparring. Train harder, get better. Yes, putting in quantity is important, but it's not as simple as that.

Here's what actually moved the needle:

1. Dropped from 6 sessions a week to 4. Quality over quantity. 4 focused, intentional sessions beat 6 sloppy, tired ones all day.

2. Added 2 strength sessions a week. Stronger legs, stronger clinch, fewer injuries. The strength work made the Muay Thai better, not the other way around.

3. Slowed everything down before I sped it up. Get it clean at half speed and the speed comes free. Rush it and you just drill in the mistakes.

4. Shadowboxed every single day, even rest days. Five minutes of flow and tight technique. Keep it simple. Best habit ever.

5. Filmed my rounds and actually watched them back. Brutal at first. But you can't fix what you can't see, and the camera doesn't lie.

6. Stopped sparring hard and started sparring smart. Hard sparring has its place, but light, technical rounds are the key. They teach you more and keep you healthy enough to keep training.

7. Fixed my stance before adding anything fancy. Everything is built on the base. Bad stance, and every technique on top of it leaks power.

8. Got 8 hours sleep instead of grinding tired. The most underrated training tool there is. Skills consolidate while you sleep.

9. Stopped chasing power and worked on timing instead. A clean shot at the right moment beats a heavy one that lands late. Timing wins fights.

10. Focused on defense as much as offense. You can't hit what you can't catch, and you can't win if you're always getting hit. Defense buys you everything.

None of this is flashy. That's kind of the point. The fundamentals win.

The answer to your Muay Thai questions 👇

But first Save this one so you can come back to it.

1️⃣ What should my training schedule look like?

3 to 4 days of Muay Thai. 2 to 3 days of strength or conditioning. One real rest day. That's the baseline. As you progress, swap one of the conditioning days for HIIT to sharpen your gas tank.

2️⃣ Should I lift weights? How often?

Yes. 2 to 3 days a week. Focus on compound lifts and explosive movements. Squats, deadlifts, presses, pull-ups, plyos. You're not trying to look like a bodybuilder. You're building force you can put behind your shots.

3️⃣ How do I condition my shins?

Kick the bag. That's it. No rolling glass bottles. No kicking trees. Just consistent, progressive bag work over months and years. Your shins adapt to the work you put in.

4️⃣ What gym should I train at in Thailand?

Depends what you want.

Phuket and Koh Samui: bigger gyms, English-speaking coaches, easier to land in as a first-timer. Beach lifestyle on top of training.

Bangkok: traditional gyms in the heart of the sport. Closer to the stadium scene. Less tourist polish, more raw Muay Thai culture.

Chiang Mai: smaller, quieter, more affordable. Great if you want to train hard without the party scene.

Isaan (the northeast): where most Thai fighters actually come from. Old-school camps, full immersion, not built for tourists. For serious students who want the real thing.

The wrong question is "what's the best gym." The right question is "what fits how I want to train."

5️⃣ How do I stop flinching?

Flinching is your brain protecting you. You don't fix it by trying harder. You fix it with reps under controlled pressure. Start with light technical sparring. Eyes open, react instead of pull away. Build speed over weeks, not minutes.

Drill defense in isolation. Slips, parries, checks. The more your body knows what to do, the less your brain panics. It fades. But only with time on the mat.

7 tests. Most guys fail 4 of them.

Not because they're not trying. Because they're training without structure.

1️⃣ You train when you don't feel like it.

2️⃣ You've watched your own footage in the last month.

3️⃣ You can name your biggest technical weakness right now.

4️⃣ You light spar more than you hard spar.

Every guy starting Muay Thai in his 30s or 40s asks the same question...

Am I too old.

You're not.

You're just on a different timeline than the 22 year old next to you.

Here's the timeline that works:
✅ Train 3 to 4 times a week.
✅ Light spar way more than you hard spar.
✅ Get on a structured program.
✅ Recover like it's a session.

Do that for a year and you'll surprise yourself.

The Muay Thai newb evolution 👇

Month one: bought the gloves, the shorts, the shin guards, the hand wraps in three colors, and a jump rope they will never use.

Month two: skipping clinch, skipping warm ups, sparring like every round is a title fight.

Month three: giving the new guy technique tips they got off a YouTube short.

Month four: ghost the gym because they got tapped in sparring and their ego can't take it.

The ones who make it past month six all have one thing in common.

They stopped trying to look like a fighter and started training like one.

Am I missing anything?

Some days I don't want to train.

Not because I'm lazy. Because I'm tired in a way that goes deeper than physical. Dad tired. Work tired. The kind of tired where the couch wins every argument.

But I've learned something after almost 20 years of doing this.

The days I least want to train are the days I need it most.

Not for fitness. Not for the physique. Because of who I am when I don't train consistently.

More irritable. Less patient. Shorter fuse with my kids. Less present with my wife. Stuck in my head in a way I can't shake.

Muay Thai is not just my workout. It's the thing that keeps everything else running. My mental health. My physical health. My ability to show up as a father and a husband without running on empty.

When I take care of that hour, everything else gets a better version of me.

My kids get a dad who comes home with energy instead of bringing the weight of the day through the door.

My wife gets a husband who's present instead of distracted.

I get to feel like myself.

It took me a long time to stop feeling guilty about protecting that time. To stop framing it as selfish and start understanding it as necessary.

You can't pour from an empty cup. I know that sounds like a fridge magnet. It's also just true.
If you're a parent who's been putting your training last, here are three things that actually helped me stay consistent.

Protect one session like a meeting you cannot cancel. Just one. Build from there.
Tell your partner why it matters. Not just that you want to train. Why it makes you better at home. That conversation changes things.

Lower the bar on the hard days. Twenty minutes is enough. Showing up is enough. You don't have to crush every session. You just have to keep the habit alive.

Take care of yourself. Your family needs you to.

Nobody warned me about any of this... especially the last few 👇

1 . The learning curve is steeper than it looks and lasts longer than you expect. Plan for a year before it starts feeling natural.

2. Your cardio will betray you in round one for the first six months. This is normal. Push through it.

3. You will be the worst person in the room for a while. That's not a problem. That's the whole point.

4. Your ego will take more damage than your body early on. Both will recover.

5. The warm up is not optional at your age. Skipping it is just scheduling an injury for next week.

6. You will cancel plans for training and feel zero guilt about it. This happens faster than you think.

7. Progress is invisible for months and then suddenly it isn't. Do not quit in the invisible phase.

8. Your non-training friends will not understand why you do this. That's fine. You're not doing it for them.

9. The technique that feels impossible today will be automatic in a year. Everything clicks eventually.

10. Starting late is not a disadvantage. Adults learn differently, not worse. You bring discipline and patience that 22 year olds don't have yet.

Most people train for years and never figure these out.

Which "secret" changed your training the most? Drop it below.

These look like you're slacking... but they are the smartest things you can do 👇

1. Shadowboxing at 50% speed. Looks like you're barely trying. Actually burning in technique, building muscle memory, and training your brain to see openings instead of just reacting. Don't get me wrong, there's a time and place for 100%, but most of the time slow = fast. 

2 . Sitting out a hard sparring round to watch. Looks like you're avoiding work. Actually studying patterns, reads, and setups you can't see when you're in the middle of it.

3. Going light when everyone else is going hard. Looks like you're taking it easy. Actually building timing, relaxation, and technique that will still be there when you're tired in round 4.

4. Taking a full rest day with no cross training. Looks lazy. Is literally training. Your body repairs and adapts during rest, not during the session.

5. Drilling the same combination for an entire session. Looks boring and limited. Is actually how you build the kind of automatic technique that works under pressure when everything else falls apart.
 
6. Spending 20 minutes on mobility before training. Looks like you're killing time. Is the reason you're still training without injuries while everyone else is nursing something.

7. Sitting in a deep squat while watching rounds instead of standing. Looks like you're just hanging out. Actually building the hip mobility that makes your kicks and teeps look effortless.

The guys who look like they're working the hardest are often improving the slowest. 

The guys who look relaxed and deliberate are the ones who get dangerous quietly.

Most people quit Muay Thai in year one.

Not because it's too hard. Because they went too hard too fast.

Six sessions a week. Two-a-days. Full send every sparring round. Zero recovery. Burned out by March.

Then nothing.

I've watched it happen more times than I can count. Guys who were more naturally talented than me, more athletic, more dedicated in those first few months. Gone within a year.

But here's the other version that kills people just as fast.

They miss one session. Then two. Then a week goes by and instead of just coming back, something shifts in their head. They tell themselves they've fallen off. That they need to restart properly. That they'll come back when things settle down at work, when the kids are back at school, when life gets less busy.

Life never gets less busy.

One missed week turns into a month. A month turns into "I used to train Muay Thai."

The all or nothing mindset is the thing that ends more training careers than any injury ever has.

Missing a week doesn't erase your progress. Missing a month doesn't mean you've failed. Showing up imperfectly is not the same as not showing up. One session when you're tired and distracted and only half present still counts. It keeps the habit alive. It keeps the identity alive.

The ones still training at 40 are not the ones who never missed a session. They're the ones who kept coming back after they did.

Train less if you have to. 
Train tired if you have to.
Train for twenty minutes if that's all you've got.
Just don't stop.

If you want a program built around showing up consistently in a real life with real interruptions, comment FBA and I'll send it over.

Imperfect consistency beats perfect intention every time.

The most underrated people in Muay Thai are the ones nobody sees coming.

I spent years training twice a day, cutting weight, preparing for fights. I genuinely thought that was the hardest thing I'd ever do physically and mentally.

Then I became a dad with a full time business, real financial responsibilities, and a body that needs actual recovery time.
I had no idea.

Training for fights is hard. But you know exactly what you're doing and why. Your whole life is structured around it. Sleep, food, sessions, recovery. That's it.

Training Muay Thai while juggling a career, kids, a mortgage, school runs, emails, dinner, and six hours of sleep on a good night is a completely different kind of hard. There's no structure handed to you. You build it yourself in the cracks of everything else.

Full time job. 
Kids at home. 
Commute.

Dinner to cook. 
Emails to answer. 
And somewhere in between all of that they still find time to train, still show up to sparring, still get better every month.

No sponsors. No highlight reel. No one clapping for them. They just do it because they decided to.
That's the whole thing. And honestly it might be more impressive than anything I did in the ring.

The Muay Thai newb starter pack...

No wraps. Full ego.
Four hundred dollars worth of gear and no idea how to throw a jab. 
Convinced they're ready to spar after two pad sessions.
Has already told six people they train Muay Thai.

We've all been there. Some of us are still there. You know who you are.

Somewhere along the way training twice a day, running before the sun comes up, and spending your free time watching fight tape became completely normal.

Not complaining. Just saying most people would think we're insane.

The funny thing is once you're in it, everything else starts to feel like the weird choice.

 Sitting on a stationary bike staring at a screen for 45 minutes? That's the strange one. 

Spending an hour shadowboxing, drilling combinations, and actually getting better at something? That makes sense.

You try to go back to the gym after a few months of training and you're just... standing there moving weights around wondering what the point is.

When oxygen is extracted from the blood to the muscle cell it needs to be utilised by oxidative enzymes.

30 s max effort sprints provide a strong signal for rapid changes in oxidative enzyme capacity and function as well as having beneficial effects on neuromuscular force generation, coordination at high speed and mental toughness.

WHY IS THE RED ZONE IMPORTANT FOR BOXING? 🥊📈

For boxers, becoming familiar with and dominating the Red Zone is important as large portions portions of competition are performed at this high intensity. 

Whilst Red Zone intensity is achieved regularly during sparring, it is often difficult to hit the Red Zone during rounds on the bags or pads. 

This is due to natural pacing strategies that have been developed from doing these rounds on the pads or bags time and time again, setting yourself up for a big finish in the last 30-15 seconds of a 3 minute round.

To address this and get the most out of technical work form a conditioning perspective breaking three minute rounds up into intervals facilitates higher intensities and Red Zone DOMINANCE 🔥‼️

We are more than just coaches.

We are mentors, teachers, and steady voices when doubt gets loud. We are the push when motivation fades and the belief when confidence feels far away. A coach doesn’t just build athletes ,we help build people. We see potential before it’s fully formed. We challenge limits. We teach discipline, resilience, and accountability. The lessons go far beyond the gym, the field, or the ring. They carry into life. As a fight coach in boxing and Muay Thai, I’ve come to understand something deeply. Combat sports can be one of the loneliest journeys in the world. You train with a team. You laugh, grind, and grow together. But when it’s time to step through the ropes, it’s just you your breath, your thoughts, your heart beating in your chest. In those quiet moments before the bell, every doubt tries to speak up. That’s where the real growth lives. That’s where character is revealed. Along this path, people enter your life who change you. Training partners become family. Coaches become guiding lights. Students don’t just learn from you they teach you patience, perspective, and purpose. You sweat together. You struggle together. You rise together. You watch each other evolve not only as fighters, but as human beings. And sometimes, the hardest part of the journey isn’t the fight itself.

Sometimes, paths separate. Not because of anger. Not because of failure. But because growth can lead people in different directions, toward new goals and new seasons in life. And that’s okay. Because every person you share this journey with leaves a mark. They help shape you, sharpen you, and build the version of you standing here today — stronger, wiser, and more grounded. That’s the true fight game. Not just training and competition, but connection, growth, and learning when to let go with respect and gratitude. So yes we are more than just coaches. We are part of the journey. And the journey is what creates champions in sport and in life.

Being nervous before your first fight is completely normal. I still get nervous myself, and honestly, that’s not a bad thing.

The goal isn’t to eliminate fear. It’s to learn how to perform even when you feel nervous. And with every fight, you get better at handling it.

Here’s what helped me the most:

1. Stop overthinking the worst-case scenario.

Your mind can create a hundred different situations that will probably never happen. Instead of worrying about things you can’t control, focus on what you can control: your preparation and your work.

2. Trust your preparation.

You don’t have to be perfect. You just need to know you’ve put in the work and prepared yourself for the challenge ahead.

3. Focus on learning, not just winning.

Don’t put too much pressure on yourself to look like a professional from day one. Your first fight is about gaining experience and learning how to handle real pressure. Win or lose, you’ll learn something that makes you better.

4. Learn to be comfortable with discomfort.

Hard sparring, intense pad work, conditioning and competition training help you stay calm when your heart is racing and things get difficult.

5. Keep your game plan simple.

Don’t try to remember 20 different techniques. Focus on your fundamentals: how you want to start, what you want to land, how you’ll defend and what to do when things don’t go as planned.

You’ll probably still feel nervous when you walk into the ring or cage. That’s okay.

Take a breath, trust your training and fight the way you’ve prepared to fight.

Your first fight doesn’t have to be perfect. It’s about learning, gaining experience and having the courage to step in there.
